content: Mpox is a disease caused by infection with the mpox virus. In 2022, an outbreak occurred globally in regions where mpox is not typically found. Historically, mpox was primarily observed in Central and West Africa, often in forested areas. Individuals infected with mpox develop a rash that may initially resemble pimples or blisters. This rash is usually painful. Symptoms of Mpox The symptoms of mpox include the following: A rash that may initially appear as pimples or blisters. The rash can be painful or itchy. It may be located on or near the genitals (penis, testicles, labia, and vagina), anus, or other areas such as the hands, feet, chest, face, or mouth. The rash progresses through several stages, including the formation of scabs, before healing. The illness typically lasts 2 to 4 weeks. How Mpox Spreads Mpox can spread through close, personal, often skin-to-skin contact, including: Direct contact with the rash, scabs, or bodily fluids (such as saliva or respiratory secretions) of an infected person. Contact with areas around the anus, rectum, or vagina of an infected individual. Intimate contact, such as oral, anal, or vaginal sex, or touching the genitals or anus of someone with mpox. Hugging, massaging, or kissing. Prolonged face-to-face contact. The virus can also spread by touching objects, fabrics, or surfaces that have been used by someone with mpox and not disinfected, such as clothing, bedding, or towels. However, the risk of transmission through these means is considered relatively low. Who Is at Risk? Anyone in close contact with a person infected with mpox is at risk and should take precautions, including vaccination. Data from the 2022 outbreak suggests that gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men represent the majority of cases. Individuals who engage in close, skin-to-skin contact with someone infected are at higher risk. Caregivers of individuals with mpox should avoid direct skin-to-skin contact with the infected person, wash their hands frequently, and use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), such as masks and gloves, when providing care. They should not share eating utensils or cups and should avoid handling bedding, towels, or clothing of infected individuals. Caregivers are advised to consider getting vaccinated against mpox. Travelers, such as veterinarians and wildlife professionals, may be at risk if they work with infected animals, particularly in regions where wild animals are known to carry the virus, such as Central and West Africa. Preventive Measures for Travelers To avoid contracting mpox, travelers should take the following precautions: Get two doses of the mpox vaccine before traveling. Avoid close, skin-to-skin contact with individuals who have a rash resembling mpox. Do not touch the rash or scabs of an infected person. Avoid kissing, hugging, cuddling, or having sex with someone who has mpox. Avoid contact with objects and materials used by an infected person, such as bedding, towels, clothing, or sex toys. Do not share eating utensils or cups with an infected person. Wash your hands frequently with soap and water or use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer, especially before eating, touching your face, or after using the bathroom. What to Do If You Have Mpox Symptoms or Have Been Exposed If you develop symptoms of mpox or have been in contact with someone infected, you should isolate yourself at home or another location until your symptoms resolve and your rash has completely healed. This means all scabs must have fallen off, and a fresh layer of skin must have formed. If you have mpox and must travel: Ensure you do not have a fever or respiratory symptoms such as a sore throat, nasal congestion, or cough. Cover your rash and wear a well-fitting mask. Additional Travel Considerations If you test positive for mpox while at an international destination, you may be subject to local public health laws and regulations. These may include isolation requirements and restrictions on travel until you are no longer considered contagious. If you have been in contact with someone with mpox and travel internationally, you may also be subject to local public health laws, including restrictions on travel until you are no longer at risk of developing mpox. If you exhibit symptoms of mpox, you may be required to isolate and undergo testing for the virus. Check the relevant government websites for information on arrival procedures and public health guidelines.
